Fashion Demand Forecast

Evaluating Google Trends as a demand signal for US clothing retail forecasting

View Repository →
Python statsmodels Prophet pandas pytest FRED API GitHub Actions

The Problem

Clothing retail sales follow strong seasonal patterns, but understanding whether online search behavior adds predictive value beyond historical seasonality remains unclear. Google Trends provides search interest data for fashion categories, but its utility as a leading indicator for aggregate monthly retail sales is untested. Retailers and forecasters need to know if investing in exogenous data sources improves forecast accuracy over baseline methods.

What Was Built

  • Built a comparative forecasting pipeline that evaluates five model variants across 12-fold rolling-window cross-validation with a 10-year initial training window and 12-month forecast horizon.
  • Fetched 20+ years of US clothing retail sales from FRED (MRTSSM448USN) and deflated nominal values to real dollars using CPI Apparel index, isolating demand changes from price inflation.
  • Collected Google Trends data for six fashion market segments (fast fashion, luxury, sustainable, couture, secondhand, discount) as potential exogenous regressors.
  • Implemented three model classes: SeasonalNaive (baseline that repeats last year's values), SARIMAXModel (statsmodels wrapper with configurable order), and ProphetModel (lazy import to avoid test dependencies).
  • Designed rolling-window cross-validation in evaluation.py with 1-year steps, producing 12 train/test splits that span pre-recession, Great Recession, recovery, and COVID-19 periods.
  • Compared each model with and without Google Trends regressors to isolate the contribution of search interest data, using RMSE, MAE, and MAPE as evaluation metrics.

Outcome

Prophet without Google Trends achieved the lowest mean RMSE (2,145) across 12 cross-validation folds, outperforming the seasonal naive baseline. Adding Google Trends degraded both SARIMAX and Prophet by 2.7% and 11.5% respectively, demonstrating that monthly search interest for fashion categories does not improve forecast accuracy over historical seasonality alone. The analysis pipeline runs 29 tests in CI without external API dependencies, and all figures and metrics are reproducible via notebooks/analysis.ipynb.

Highlights

Rolling-window cross-validation design

Implemented 12-fold time series cross-validation with a 10-year initial training window and 1-year step, producing train/test splits that span structural breaks including the Great Recession and COVID-19 crash. This design (in evaluation.py) provides more robust performance estimates than a single train/test split, as it evaluates models across different economic regimes and seasonal patterns. Each fold trains on a different historical window and forecasts the subsequent 12 months, aggregating RMSE, MAE, and MAPE across all folds.

Inflation adjustment with CPI Apparel

Deflated nominal clothing sales to real dollars using the CPI Apparel index (preprocessing.py), isolating actual demand changes from price inflation. Nominal sales trend upward over time due to inflation, which biases forecasts if not corrected. The deflation step divides nominal sales by the ratio of current CPI to base-year CPI, ensuring the target variable reflects quantity and volume changes rather than price level shifts. This preprocessing decision directly impacts model training and evaluation accuracy.

CI-safe test suite
  • Structured 29 tests to run without FRED API keys or external data dependencies, enabling GitHub Actions CI on every push.
  • Tests use synthetic fixtures (sample_sales, sample_cpi in test_preprocessing.py) and in-memory data, avoiding network calls.
  • Prophet imports are lazy (inside class methods in models.py), so tests that only exercise SeasonalNaive or SARIMAX do not require Prophet installation.
  • This design ensures continuous validation of core logic (metrics, preprocessing, model interfaces) without external service reliability constraints.
Exogenous regressor isolation strategy

The model comparison isolates the contribution of Google Trends by running each model (SARIMAX, Prophet) twice: once with and once without the six search interest columns as exogenous regressors. This paired design controls for model architecture, hyperparameters, and training data, attributing performance differences solely to the presence of Trends signals. The results show that Trends-augmented variants consistently underperform their baseline counterparts, demonstrating that the search terms capture general interest rather than purchase intent at monthly aggregation.

Results

Cross-validation metrics comparison

Prophet without Trends achieved the lowest mean RMSE (2,145) across 12 folds, followed by Seasonal Naive (2,351). Adding Google Trends degraded Prophet by 11.5% (RMSE = 2,391) and SARIMAX by 2.7% (RMSE = 2,844 vs. 2,770). Mean MAPE ranged from 12.0% (Prophet) to 13.9% (SARIMAX + Trends).

Metrics: Prophet: RMSE=2145, MAE=1676, MAPE=12.0% | SARIMAX: RMSE=2770, MAE=2110, MAPE=13.8% | Seasonal Naive: RMSE=2351, MAE=1779, MAPE=12.3%

COVID-19 forecast robustness

The five panels in the COVID robustness chart show actual vs. predicted sales for each model during the March-April 2020 crash. All models failed to predict the collapse (actual sales dropped from ~18,000 to ~3,000 million USD), but Prophet recovered fastest in subsequent months. Prophet + Trends overestimated recovery, showing the model learned noisy patterns from search data that did not generalize to the pandemic shock.

Metrics: Seasonal Naive RMSE during COVID: 7827 | SARIMAX: 8276 | SARIMAX + Trends: 8172 | Prophet: 7925 | Prophet + Trends: 8131

Per-fold RMSE stability

The line chart shows RMSE for each of the 12 cross-validation folds across time. All models exhibit a sharp spike around January 2020 (COVID-19 onset), with RMSE exceeding 10,000. Outside of this anomaly, Prophet maintains the most consistent RMSE (below 2,000), while Seasonal Naive shows higher variance in earlier folds. This demonstrates that Prophet's built-in handling of trend and seasonality generalizes better across different time periods.

Metrics: Prophet mean RMSE (excluding COVID fold): ~1200 | Seasonal Naive: ~1500

Forecast comparison (24-month holdout)

Overlaid forecasts from all five models on the final 24 months (Feb 2024 to Jan 2026) show Prophet and Seasonal Naive tracking actual values most closely, while Prophet + Trends diverges significantly, overforecasting by up to 5,000 million USD in some months. SARIMAX variants follow the seasonal pattern but lag the trend. The vertical dashed line marks the train/test split.

Metrics: Holdout RMSE: Prophet=2922, SARIMAX=3323, Seasonal Naive=3447, SARIMAX+Trends=3512, Prophet+Trends=8162

Nominal vs. real sales divergence

The dual-line plot shows nominal sales trending upward more steeply than real (CPI-adjusted) sales over 2004-2026, illustrating the effect of apparel price inflation. Real sales flatten during the Great Recession and crash in 2020, while nominal sales mask some of these dynamics. This preprocessing step is critical for isolating actual demand from price effects.

Google Trends correlation with sales

The heatmap shows moderate positive correlations (0.34-0.41) between real clothing sales and most fashion search terms, except couture (negative correlation: -0.13). However, inter-term correlations are high (e.g., fast fashion and sustainable fashion: 0.86), suggesting multicollinearity. Despite these correlations, the predictive value is negligible, as CV results demonstrate.

Metrics: Pearson correlation: fast_fashion=0.41, luxury_fashion=0.34, sustainable_fashion=0.38, couture=-0.13

Raw sales time series with recessions

The 1992-2026 time series shows strong annual seasonality (December spikes) and two major structural breaks: the Great Recession (2007-2009, shaded gray) caused a gradual decline, while COVID-19 (Feb-Apr 2020, shaded red) produced a near-zero collapse. Sales recovered to pre-pandemic levels by 2021, then continued growing. This chart establishes the historical volatility that models must handle.

Metrics: Peak nominal sales: ~42,000M USD (Dec 2019, Dec 2024) | COVID trough: ~3,000M USD (Apr 2020)

Google Trends temporal patterns

The six search terms show distinct temporal dynamics: luxury fashion spiked 2008-2012 then declined, fast fashion and sustainable fashion both rose post-2020, couture remained flat with high volatility, and secondhand fashion surged 2020-2024. These patterns reflect shifting consumer interest but do not translate to improved forecasts, suggesting that aggregate search interest is decoupled from purchasing behavior at monthly resolution.
